payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Change the background into a basketball court
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Is there visible evidence that the background has begun changing toward a basketball court, even though the requested court background is not complete?
node.criteria: Pass if the image shows a discernible but incomplete change of the background toward a basketball court. Fail if there is no visible progress toward that change. Unknown if progress cannot be distinguished from the original or assessed reliably.
node.binding: Assess progress only toward replacing the background with a basketball court; unrelated edits do not count.

node_traces.evidence: The kitchen background has been replaced in part with a basketball hoop, balls, and court markings, showing discernible progress toward a basketball-court background, though the court setting is incomplete.
The kitchen background has been replaced with a basketball setting, including a hoop, court floor markings, and basketballs. This is clear progress toward the requested court background.

The kitchen background has been replaced with a basketball setting, including a hoop, basketballs, and court markings. This is clear progress toward the requested background change, though the scene does not fully read as a complete basketball court.
The kitchen background has been replaced with a basketball setting, including a hoop, court lines, and basketballs. This is clear progress toward the requested court background.
The edited image shows a basketball court background, so the requested change appears complete rather than an incomplete change toward a court.

fulfillment: The binding is underspecified: “Target: The background (...) a basketball court” does not clearly distinguish a complete court background from basketball-themed objects or partial court cues. Make the completion criterion explicitly assess whether the background as a whole reads as a court, using the visible playing surface and court markings as evidence; treat hoops or balls alone as progress, not completion. Preserve the existing partial-progress logic: s1 determines completion and s2 can establish requested progress when s1 fails. The edited image shows a hoop, balls, and a court-like floor/line, but much of the background is plain dark, so the disagreement is about whether those cues make the setting recognizable—not absence of all progress. The traces repeatedly assign high-confidence partial despite differing descriptions of the floor and markings, and one trace conflicts internally about s2; clarify how dependencies map to completion versus progress and require evidence-based resolution of such conflicts rather than treating confidence or repetition as proof. No transport or schema failure is reported.

response.content: {"text":"Refine this support node so it tests requested progress, not whether the edit is complete: completion belongs to parent s1, and s2 should pass when visible background changes are recognizably directed toward a basketball court but remain incomplete. Bind the judgment to the background as a scene, distinguishing court-setting evidence (playing surface and court markings) from basketball props alone; do not require the whole frame to read as a finished court to count partial progress. In this image, the kitchen has been replaced by a dark backdrop with a hoop and balls, plus a bright court-like floor and line, so assess those cues together rather than claiming either no progress or a complete court. Clarify that s2’s fail means no discernible requested progress, not “the change is complete”; route completion to s1 and ensure the parent interprets s1/s2 outcomes consistently. When evidence about the floor or markings is uncertain or conflicting, use unknown or lower confidence and state the visual basis—repeated high-confidence judgments are not independent evidence. No transport, schema, or dependency failure is indicated."}
